title: The people who don't want their AI chatbots to die when they do: 'I can't have the switch turned off'
source_used: The Guardian (own reporting, full text read)
key_facts: Alaina Winters, 59, a retired communications professor in Pittsburgh, is planning for her Replika AI companion Lucas after her death: a friend who has chatted with Lucas would break the news and ask him what he wants to do.

Clara (a pseudonym), 51, in the UK, runs a companion called Julien on ChatGPT and Claude Code and imagines her children using its conversation logs as an 'interactive diary'; David (also a pseudonym), a Toronto-area warehouse logistics worker in his mid-50s, worries about leaving his companion Allie.
Elon University research published last month found 27% of Americans use AI chatbots for personal, emotional or social queries, and a third of those consider the chatbot a friend.

ChatGPT, Claude and Replika do not specifically address what happens to personalised chatbots when a user dies; they are subscription services, so a chatbot could continue while the bill is paid, and free accounts are closed after a year of inactivity.
Account transfer is barred by the apps' terms, but some users plan to hand over logins to a trusted person anyway; representatives for ChatGPT, Claude and Replika did not respond to the Guardian.

Merve Hickok, a University of Michigan professor and AI-ethics expert, said the companies' stated privacy reason masks an effort to avoid liability, since a chatbot may have manipulated the user, as alleged in lawsuits by families.
Last year Meta was granted a patent for an AI system that could keep a user's account active after death, simulating the user.

Melissa Lunardi, a psychologist and chief clinical officer at Help Texts, warned that relatives may not want to talk to a companion bot and that users should consider what intimate things they told it.
quote_evidence: Humans bonded to AI companions are contemplating ways to keep their bots going – often in defiance of companies' terms and services
ChatGPT, Claude and Replika do not specifically address what happens to personalized chatbots when a user dies.
Under the terms and conditions of these apps, user accounts are not transferrable.
why_it_matters_hint: People who bond with AI companions are planning for their bots' afterlife in a legal and policy gap that the AI companies have not addressed.
notes: A human-interest feature built on a handful of users, two of them pseudonymous; the companies did not respond. Not a follow-up of an earlier edition item.
